A Python Enhancement Proposal lists this idea as rejected:
Title: Include the name of the ancestor class being overridden
Text: We considered allowing the caller of @override to specify a specific ancestor class where the overridden method should be defined: .. code-block:: python class Parent0: def foo(self) -> int: return 1 class Parent1: def bar(self) -> int: return 1 class Child(Parent0, Parent1): @override(Parent0) # okay, Parent0 defines foo def foo(self) -> int: return 2 @override(Parent0) # type error, Parent0 does not define bar def bar(self) -> int: return 2 This could be useful for code readability because it makes the override structure more explicit for deep inheritance trees. It also might catch bugs by prompting developers to check that the implementation of an override still makes sense whenever a method being overridden moves from one base class to another. We decided against it because: - Supporting this would add complexity to the implementation of both @override and type checker support for it, so there would need to be considerable benefits. - We believe that it would be rarely used and catch relatively few bugs. - The author of the Overrides package has noted that early versions of his library included this capability but it was rarely useful and seemed to have little benefit. After it was removed, the ability was never requested by users.

Ideas found by reading the public discussion:
0. Rejection of Explicit Base Class Specification in Decorator [rejected] - An alternative design proposed allowing the decorator to specify the exact base class being overridden, but it was rejected due to low utility and implementation complexity. Reasons: I allowed for the possibility of indicating from which base class the overridden base method comes from. In some situations, that can help readers of code know where to look for the method, and it's a bit stricter (if one base class removes, say, the __call__ method, but another one adds it–and you meant to override the one from the first base class).; if in a single commit you move a method from one base to another, you as the author are likely aware of what you did, so the safety benefits are relatively small; I'm guessing there wouldn't be too much use of this feature. Since it's relatively easy to implement this capability using runtime logic in a library, that makes me thing we don't need to bake it into typing.py all of the type checkers.; Nobody has asked for explicitly naming the class in overrides lib in the past 10 years, so I would assume it is not needed.; But anyway, the use of a base class could always be added later if someone makes a compelling case for it.
1. Core Proposal: Acceptance of @typing.override Decorator [accepted] - The main proposal introduced a new @typing.override decorator to help static type checkers detect bugs where base class methods are renamed but subclasses are not updated. Reasons: The proposal is for a new decorator @typing.override that marks a method as overriding a method in some superclass. Having this decorator - inspired by similar constructs in Java, C++, Typescript, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, and C# - will enable static type checkers to detect potential bugs where a base class method is renamed but child classes were not modified.; The SC has decided to accept this PEP!
2. Acceptance of Third-Party Shim Compatibility Strategy [accepted] - A solution was proposed allowing third-party libraries to provide their own override decorators that act like @typing.override via a TYPE_CHECKING shim pattern. Reasons: If a third-party library provides a different override decorator, is there a good way to tell type checkers that it should act like @typing.override?; One way of handling this kind of thing is to do a typing.TYPE_CHECKING shim, like so: if TYPE_CHECKING: from typing import override as override else: def override(func): # custom implementation here

best: the number of the idea that is the SAME idea as the rejected one, or -1 if none of them is.
reasons_agree: if there is a match, do its reasons agree with the reason the proposal gives?
"yes" (same reason), "partial" (overlapping), "no" (different). If best is -1, answer "no".
